questions.question: How is $x^{1/n}$ defined?
options: As the infimum of all real y such that y^n ≥ x
As any real number y satisfying y^n = x
As the supremum of all real y such that y ≥ 0 and y^n ≤ x
As the average of x and n
questions.explanation: For $x\ge0$, the definition sets $x^{1/n}=\sup\{y\in\mathbb R:y\ge0,\ y^n\le x\}$. Completeness supplies the supremum.
questions.source_support: The definition states x^($\frac{1}{n}$) = sup{y in R: y ≥ 0 and y^n ≤ x}.

questions.question: Using the course convention for odd roots, what is $(-8)^{1/3}$?
options: It is not real.
questions.explanation: An odd power is one-to-one on the real line, so every real input has one real odd root. Since $(-2)^3=-8$, the real cube root is $-2$.
questions.source_support: For odd $n$, the real $n$-th root is defined for every real input.

Negative numbers do have real odd roots; only even roots require a nonnegative real input.
An odd root is single-valued over the reals; only $-2$, not both signs, cubes to $-8$.

questions.explanation: The principal square root is the nonnegative number whose square is $4$. Since $2^2=4$, $\sqrt4=2$.
questions.source_support: The square root is the non-negative inverse of squaring for non-negative inputs.

questions.question: Which monotonicity property does the $n$-th root function have on $[0,+\infty)$?
options: It is decreasing on $[0,+\infty)$.
It is increasing only when $n$ is even.

questions.question: Which statement gives the real-domain rule for $n$-th roots when $n$ is a positive integer?
options: Every positive integer index allows every real input $x$.
Every positive integer index requires a nonnegative input $x$.
Even indices allow all real inputs; odd indices require $x\ge0$.
Even indices require $x\ge0$; odd indices allow every real $x$.
questions.explanation: Even powers cannot produce negative real values, so even roots need a nonnegative input. Odd powers cover all real values, so odd roots are defined for every real input.
questions.source_support: Even roots require nonnegative inputs, whereas odd roots are real-valued on all of $\mathbb R$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Updated the domain item to distinguish even and odd roots.
option_explanations: Even indices do not allow negative real inputs, because an even power is nonnegative.
Odd indices allow negative inputs, for example $\sqrt[3]{-8}=-2$.
This reverses the parity rule: even roots, not odd roots, need $x\ge0$.
